title: Owner-scoped idempotency and durable request identity
note: Every mutation here removes one thing that keeps an idempotency key a NAME rather than an AUTHORITY. The scope (owner, tool, key) is what makes a guessed string unreachable; the owner coming from the event rather than the payload is what stops a binding choosing whose namespace it lives in; the rebinding refusal is what stops a second request inheriting the first one's identity. The production mutations remove the suppression itself, which is the failure that runs the work twice while reporting that it did not.

mutations.name: I1_the_owner_is_taken_from_the_payload
mutations.find: if claimed_owner is not None and claimed_owner != actor:
mutations.rationale: a forged binding names whoever it likes as its owner, so it chooses whose key namespace to write into and a later lookup hands that actor the attacker's task

mutations.name: I2_the_scope_drops_the_owner
mutations.rationale: the key becomes global, so guessing the string reaches another actor's task, evidence and result -- the whole reason the namespace is scoped

mutations.name: I3_the_scope_drops_the_tool
mutations.rationale: one key collides across tools, so a submission to a second tool is suppressed as a duplicate of work that ran somewhere else

mutations.name: I4_the_scope_is_a_joined_string
mutations.rationale: an owner literally named 'a:b' with key 'c' collides with owner 'a' and key 'b:c'; a separator that can appear in the values is not a separator

mutations.name: I5_a_rebinding_replaces_the_live_binding
mutations.find:
raise IdempotencyError(
                f"seq {ev.seq}: idempotency key {binding.key!r} for tool "
mutations.replace:
self._bindings[scope] = binding
            return True
            raise IdempotencyError(
                f"seq {ev.seq}: idempotency key {binding.key!r} for tool "
mutations.rationale: every later resubmission of the ORIGINAL request resolves to the attacker's task, so the original never runs and the caller is told it already did

mutations.name: I6_a_binding_may_backdate_itself
mutations.rationale: a binding appended late claims an earlier position, backdating the moment a duplicate would first have been caught

mutations.name: I7_request_identity_ignores_the_inputs
mutations.rationale: any two submissions to one tool look like the same request, so a genuinely different request is suppressed and never runs

mutations.name: I8_a_changed_request_reuses_the_binding
mutations.rationale: the key stops naming one request; a second, different request inherits the first one's identity and result

mutations.name: I9_request_identity_is_not_required_to_be_canonical
mutations.rationale: identity derived from something other than canonical bytes stops matching across a restart, which is the only time this subsystem does anything

mutations.name: I10_production_never_looks_the_key_up
mutations.rationale: every resubmission runs the work again; the binding is written and never consulted, which is duplicate suppression that suppresses nothing

mutations.name: I11_production_never_binds
mutations.rationale: nothing durable records the submission, so a resubmission after a lost response starts the work a second time

mutations.name: I12_the_lookup_takes_the_owner_from_the_tool_id
mutations.rationale: the namespace stops being per-submitter at the production boundary even though the ledger still scopes it, so two submitters share one key

mutations.name: I13_the_binding_lands_after_the_work_is_dispatched
mutations.find:
if idempotency_key:
            self.idempotency.bind(
                owner=submitter, tool_id=tool_id, key=idempotency_key,
                request_digest=request_digest, task_id=task_id,
                job_id=job_id)

        # Validation is a real gate
mutations.rationale: the window between submitting and binding is exactly the window a crash makes a duplicate; binding after dispatch does not cover it

mutations.name: I14_the_submitter_is_not_a_registered_identity
mutations.rationale: an arbitrary string becomes the policy subject and the owner of a durable key namespace

mutations.name: I15_an_external_effect_is_reported_as_a_clean_duplicate
mutations.rationale: a run that may have performed an irreversible external action and died before recording it is reported as a settled duplicate, which invents the one fact nobody has

mutations.name: I16_a_timeout_counts_as_a_settled_external_effect
mutations.rationale: a timeout is precisely the case where nothing observed the tool finish, so treating it as settled reports 'the external effect did not happen' with no basis

mutations.name: I17_the_second_reader_takes_the_last_binding_it_sees
mutations.find:
out.anomalies.append(
            f"seq {ev.seq}: idempotency key {key!r} for {tool_id!r} is "
mutations.replace:
bindings[scope] = {"key": key, "owner": ev.actor,
                           "tool_id": tool_id, "task_id": task_id,
                           "request_digest": request_digest,
                           "job_id": p.get("job_id", ""),
                           "bound_seq": ev.seq}
        return
        out.anomalies.append(
            f"seq {ev.seq}: idempotency key {key!r} for {tool_id!r} is "
mutations.rationale: the independent reader agrees with the attacker instead of disagreeing with the ledger, which is the one thing a second reader exists to prevent

mutations.name: I18_the_second_reader_trusts_the_payloads_owner
mutations.rationale: both readers now believe a forged owner, so the differential check that would have caught it agrees with itself

mutations.name: I19_the_audit_reports_the_payloads_owner
mutations.rationale: the auditor reads an attacker-controlled field and tells the reader a forged binding belonged to the honest submitter

mutations.name: I20_the_audit_stops_counting_executions
mutations.rationale: a task that ran the work twice under one identity passes audit, so 'it did not run twice' stops being checkable from the log
